summary:
Every year, floods swamp Philippine cities. Are the storms getting worse, or is something else changing beneath our feet? Earth Trend Detective is an investigative tool that treats severe flooding in five Philippine cities like a case to be solved. It puts each suspect (rising seas, sinking ground, heavier rain, overflowing rivers, warming, urbanization, typhoons and La Niña) through the same statistical test, using NASA satellites, a NASA model and ground records going back as far as 1902. It shows which factors the data supports, which it does not, and what to check or fix next.

The evidence holds surprises. Typhoon landfalls show no trend since 1951, yet Manila's sea level is rising about 139 mm per decade, nine times faster than before 1965, partly because the ground itself is sinking. NASA's model says rain is increasing, but satellites don't confirm it, and the app says so plainly.

The same detective tools work anywhere on Earth. Students can click any place on a map, choose a NASA variable and test whether its trend is real, guided by demonstrations, a glossary and an AI "Detective".
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Trend Detective is a web tool that helps students and the public find trends in NASA Earth science data and test whether they are real. Users click any point on Earth, or pick one of 15 ready-made places, and choose one of 12 variables: night-time and daytime temperature, rainfall, evaporation, soil wetness, humidity, cloud cover, sunlight and wind. These come from NASA's MERRA-2 model and CERES satellite data through the NASA POWER API. The tool turns about 45 years of monthly data (1981–2025) into a yearly time series for the whole year or a chosen season. It calculates the rate of change per decade with Sen's slope and a 95% range, tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test, and explains the result in plain language. Users can compare two places side by side, download the data as CSV, or upload their own data for the same test.

A second mode compares five Philippine cities across all our case-study datasets: GPM IMERG rainfall, MODIS land surface temperature, GLDAS runoff and soil moisture, and tide-gauge and river records. An AI assistant, the "Detective", explains any result. If the AI is unavailable, it answers from built-in rules computed from the app's own data.

Benefits

  • Students practice the full scientific workflow (choose a variable and a region, plot it, test it, interpret it) without coding or installing anything.
  • Every result says whether a change is significant, and that "not significant" often means "not enough data yet". This teaches users to check before they conclude.
  • A guided start (three questions about topic, place and season), two step-by-step demonstrations, and a glossary make the statistics approachable.

Intended impact

We applied the tool to a question that matters at home: what drives severe flooding in the Philippines? We combined NASA data with tide-gauge, typhoon, El Niño and flood records going back to 1902:

  • Manila's shoreline sea level is rising about 139 mm per decade since 1965, roughly nine times faster than before, partly because the ground is sinking.
  • Typhoon landfalls show no significant trend since 1951.
  • La Niña years bring significantly more flood deaths.

This points planners toward sinking ground, sea level, drainage and urbanization, and toward preparing harder in La Niña years. Because the tool works anywhere on Earth, students in any country can investigate their own region the same way.

Here are the variables behind each suspect, where they come from, and what the significance test found. "Significant" means the Mann-Kendall test gave p below 0.05; links to La Niña use a Spearman correlation.

In short:

  • Supported by the data: rising sea level at Manila (partly sinking ground), warming nights, and more flood deaths in La Niña years.
  • Not supported: more typhoons, more river flood events, or more recorded floods.
  • Unconfirmed: heavier rain. The NASA model says yes, but the satellite says no.
  • Not yet testable: how much urbanization and sinking ground add to flooding. That needs flood-depth maps and ground-motion (GNSS) stations, which the app lists under "What is missing".

Tools, languages and software

  • Front end: TypeScript, React and Vite. Leaflet with OpenStreetMap for the map. Our own SVG charts and statistics code (Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope).
  • Data processing: Python scripts for IBTrACS typhoon tracks, the NOAA Oceanic Niño Index, Dartmouth Flood Observatory records and GLDAS exports. Data was downloaded from NASA POWER and NASA Giovanni.
  • AI: Google Gemini, called from an AWS Lambda function so the API key never reaches the browser.
  • Hosting: AWS S3 and CloudFront (HTTPS), with DynamoDB for rate limits on AI calls. Code on GitHub.
  • Hardware: no special hardware; everything runs in a standard web browser.

Architecture: the app is a React and TypeScript web app served over HTTPS from AWS S3 and CloudFront. All the statistics (Mann-Kendall test, Sen's slope, 95% range) run in the user's browser, so results appear instantly. When a user clicks the map, the browser fetches about 45 years of monthly data straight from the NASA POWER API. Data for 15 ready-made places is saved inside the app, so the demonstrations work even if NASA's servers are slow. Python scripts turn the raw downloads (IBTrACS typhoon tracks, NOAA's El Niño index, flood records and GLDAS exports from NASA Giovanni) into data files the app reads directly. The AI Detective runs on AWS Lambda, which calls Google Gemini. The API key stays on the server, a DynamoDB table limits how often each visitor can ask, and if the AI is unavailable the Detective answers from built-in rules, so it never breaks.

Creativity

  • We framed flooding as a detective story: each possible cause is a "suspect" put through the same test.
  • One demonstration shows the challenge's hardest idea with real data. Daytime highs are falling in tropical Cagayan de Oro but rising in desert Phoenix, and cloud cover explains both.
  • Another shows how a short record can hide a real trend.
  • The AI Detective can explain any live result for a high school reader.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty: when NASA's model and satellite data disagree (for example on rainfall), the app says so instead of choosing one. Each finding lists what the data cannot tell us and which measurements would settle it.
  • Audience: plain-language definitions and explanations for high school and college students, as the challenge describes.
  • Valid statistics: a minimum of 10 years before any test, and one value per year (or the same months each year) so the seasonal cycle cannot fake a trend.
  • Reliability: data for the ready-made places is saved in the app, so the demos work even if NASA's servers are slow, and the chat always has a fallback answer.
  • Privacy and cost: uploaded files stay in the user's browser, AI calls are rate-limited, and visitors are identified only by a hashed IP address.
